newsitem.title: USA: Simpson's life story defies imagination.
newsitem.headline: Simpson's life story defies imagination.

text.p: In a stunning reversal of fortune, O.J. Simpson went from American football hero to suspected killer.
Now, acquitted of double-murder charges, he is still struggling to clear his name in the court of public opinion.

The former sports star, actor and TV personality took the witness stand on Friday in a civil trial in which he is being sued for wrongful death in the June 12, 1994 murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman.
No Hollywood screenwriter could have made up the twists and turns that led Simpson to where he stands today -- trying to convince a second jury of his innocence.

A criminal court jury acquitted Simpson more than a year ago of the murders. Having been found not guilty in the criminal case, Simpson cannot be sent to jail should the plaintiffs prevail in the civil case, but he could be forced to pay substantial damages.
Simpson's is a rags-to-riches story that captured the attention of America and, since his arrest on June 17, 1994, much of the rest of the world.
The appropriate adjective for Simpson has always been the "first." He pioneered the multi-million-dollar television endorsements that have since become commonplace for athletes.

He was the first-round pick in the 1969 National Football League draft after leading the University of Southern California to a national championship in 1968 and collecting the coveted Heisman Trophy along the way. In 1973, playing with the Buffalo Bills, he set records running with the ball.

Orenthal James Simpson was born in one of San Francisco's roughest neighbourhoods, the Potrero Hill housing projects, on July 9, 1947. As a youngster he suffered from rickets, a Vitamin D and calcium deficiency and had to wear leg braces. He recovered from the disease but it left him bowlegged.

His mother Eunice toiled long hours as a hospital technician while his father Jimmy Lee Simpson worked as a bank custodian during the day and as a porter in a private club at night. When Simpson was five his parents divorced and Eunice was left to raise him and his three siblings.
Simpson spent his teen years as a gang leader, fighting in the streets and engaging in petty crime, such as stealing pies from a bakery.
"I was somebody who didn't care about anything," Simpson once told The Los Angeles Times, "and the best thing you can say about me and trouble was that I was borderline."

Simpson credits baseball great Willie Mays with turning his life around after Simpson spent a weekend in a youth detention centre when he was 16. On his release from custody, Simpson received a surprise visit from Mays, his idol, who sometimes helped troubled youngsters.

He enrolled at San Francisco City College and then the University of California two years later. In 1969, following his success at the University of Southern California, he was the first pick in the NFL draft, starting a career with the the Bills that led to his induction in the football Hall of Fame in 1985.

Simpson married his high school sweetheart, Marguerite Whitley, in 1967, and they had three children. They split up in 1977 and divorced in 1979. Simpson met second wife Nicole Brown in June, 1977, when she was working at a popular Los Angeles night spot. He was about to turn 30, she was 18.
They married in 1985 after living together for eight years and stayed married for seven more turbulent years until their divorce in 1992. During that time they had two children.

Simpson's murder trial and the current court proceedings, which presiding Judge Hiroshi Fujiosaki described to jurors as a "civil murder trial", have given the public a portrait of him that they had never seen before: a brooding, jealous man with a fierce temper.
Many people found it hard to reconcile that image with his public persona of a talented athlete and a poised, courteous celebrity who modestly understated his achievements.
Simpson's image was carefully nutured after his football career when he stepped into the broadcasting booth as an NFL commentator and acted in about a dozen Hollywood movies.

Simpson, who spent more than 15 months in jail before his acquittal in October, 1995, has since sought to regain favour with a distrusting public, many of whom believe he literally got away with murder.

He has courted the black community, joined a Los Angeles church and made public speeches. He has also given TV interviews, made regular trips to the golf course and appeared at the Oxford University debating union in England.
In addition, Simpson made a videotaped "infomercial" explaining how he could not have committed the murders, although industry experts said it did not sell well.
